claim: On 30 May 2024 NASA's Curiosity rover drove over a rock in the Gediz Vallis channel on Mount Sharp and cracked it open, revealing yellow crystals. An instrument on the rover's arm later showed they are elemental (pure) sulfur - the first time this kind of sulfur has been found on Mars. Nearby the rover found a whole field of similar bright stones.

source_title: NASA's Curiosity Rover Discovers a Surprise in a Martian Rock (NASA/JPL release 2024-100, 18 July 2024)
quote: Scientists were stunned on May 30 when a rock that NASA’s Curiosity Mars rover drove over cracked open to reveal something never seen before on the Red Planet: yellow sulfur crystals.

extra_sources.title: Same release, photo caption
extra_sources.quote: Using an instrument on the rover’s arm, scientists later determined these crystals are elemental sulfur — and it’s the first time this kind of sulfur has been found on the Red Planet.

extra_sources.title: Same release, on what 'pure' means
extra_sources.quote: But where past detections have been of sulfur-based minerals — in other words, a mix of sulfur and other materials — the rock Curiosity recently cracked open is made of elemental, or pure, sulfur.

extra_sources.title: Same release, project scientist Ashwin Vasavada (NASA JPL)
extra_sources.quote: “Finding a field of stones made of pure sulfur is like finding an oasis in the desert,” said Curiosity’s project scientist, Ashwin Vasavada of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “It shouldn’t be there, so now we have to explain it.

extra_sources.title: Same release, on the location
extra_sources.quote: Gediz Vallis channel, a groove that winds down part of the 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) Mount Sharp

extra_sources.title: Curiosity Views Sulfur Crystals Within a Crushed Rock (NASA Photojournal PIA26309, added 18 July 2024)
extra_sources.quote: Nicknamed "Convict Lake" after a location in California's Sierra Nevada, this collection of fragments is about 5 inches (13 centimeters) across from left to right.

extra_sources.title: NASA's Curiosity Mars Rover Takes a Last Look at Mysterious Sulfur (NASA/JPL release 2024-160, 18 Nov 2024)
extra_sources.quote: Science instruments on the rover confirmed the stone was pure sulfur — something no mission has seen before on Mars.

notes: All parts of the draft confirmed. Be precise about 'first': Mars rovers had found plenty of sulfur before, but always bound up in minerals such as sulfates (salts that form as water evaporates); this is the first PURE sulfur. The crystals were seen at once but identified as sulfur 'later', with APXS. The 13 cm is the size of the crushed fragments in one image, not of a single crystal; NASA gives no crystal size. The stones were too small and brittle to drill, so the team drilled a larger nearby rock, 'Mammoth Lakes' (Curiosity's 41st hole). Fun fact from the same release: although people link sulfur with the smell of rotten eggs, 'elemental sulfur is odorless'. As of NASA's Nov 2024 release the cause was still a mystery: "The team doesn't have a ready explanation for why the sulfur formed there" (I did not look for later papers). Vasavada's quote continues: "Discovering strange and unexpected things is what makes planetary exploration so exciting." The release is mirrored at nasa.gov/missions/mars-science-laboratory/curiosity-rover/nasas-curiosity-rover-discovers-a-surprise-in-a-martian-rock/; the older science.nasa.gov/missions/msl/... address returns 404.

Prefer the 2014 caption (the original measurement from the image) and keep the word 'about'; if you want to avoid the conflict, say 'one to two metres wide'. The 2014 caption calls Lebanon an 'iron meteorite' and does not mention nickel; NASA's 2025 blog groups Lebanon and Cacao among Curiosity's 'iron-nickel meteorites'. Egg Rock's 'first' is narrow: it was 'the first on Mars examined with a laser-firing spectrometer' - Spirit and Opportunity had found iron meteorites on Mars years earlier (the 2014 caption calls Lebanon 'similar in shape and luster to iron meteorites found on Mars by the previous generation of rovers, Spirit and Opportunity'), so do not say Curiosity found the first meteorite on Mars. Cacao was found in the 'sulfate-bearing unit' on Mount Sharp; its 30 cm is an estimate. Egg Rock was first noticed after an Oct. 27 drive; the release gives no sol. Origin, in the 2025 blog's words: 'iron-nickel meteorites formed in the core of large asteroids'.

claim: In 2012, during its first 40 days on Mars, Curiosity photographed two rock outcrops, 'Hottah' and 'Link', made of gravel cemented together (a rock called conglomerate). Many of the pebbles are rounded, which happens when flowing water carries them a long way and they knock against each other; they were too big to have been moved by wind. From the pebble sizes, scientists worked out that the stream flowed at about 3 feet (about 1 m) per second - at least walking pace - and was between ankle-deep and hip-deep.

notes: Every part of the draft confirmed. The speed-and-depth quote is by William Dietrich (University of California, Berkeley), a Curiosity co-investigator; the walking-pace wording is from the 2013 release, which calls it a minimum ('At a minimum'), so say 'at least walking pace' or 'about walking pace'. 0.9 m/s is the conversion of 3 ft/s; the 2013 release rounds to 'a meter'. Not every pebble is round: "Some are angular, but many are rounded." Dietrich also said: "This is the first time we're actually seeing water-transported gravel on Mars." The stones are 'cemented into a layer of conglomerate rock'; nice comparison from the 2012 release: "Hottah looks like someone jack-hammered up a slab of city sidewalk, but it's really a tilted block of an ancient streambed." The site lies between the north rim of Gale Crater and the base of Mount Sharp. The 2013 paper adds a third rock, 'Goulburn', next to the landing site; flow lasted 'certainly more than weeks or months'.

claim: In August and September 2016 Curiosity drove for just over a month among the Murray Buttes on lower Mount Sharp: flat-topped hills (buttes and mesas) up to about 15 m (50 feet) high. They are eroded remains of ancient sandstone made of sand that wind piled up as moving sand dunes. Their tops are capped with rock that resists wind erosion, so they survived while the layer around them wore away.

NASA heights for individual hills range from about 8 m to 15 m (26 to 50 feet); there is no single height for 'the Murray Buttes', so use 'up to about 15 m (50 feet)' or 'about 10 to 15 m'; any building comparison is your own. The 200-foot (60 m) figure is the ledge near the top of one mesa, not the length of the whole hill. The formation story is NASA's: wind-blown dune sand became sandstone (the 'Stimson formation') after lower Mount Sharp had formed, was buried, changed by groundwater, then exposed and eroded; an erosion-resistant cap protects each butte, 'just as is the case with many similarly shaped buttes and mesas on Earth' (PIA20840). NASA compares the scenery to the U.S. Southwest and National Parks. The farewell image caption gives the date 'Sept. 8, 2016, the 1,454th Martian day, or sol'.

claim: The Moon is slowly shrinking as its still-hot interior cools: over the last several hundred million years it has got more than about 50 m (150 feet) 'skinnier'. Just as a grape wrinkles as it shrinks down to a raisin, the Moon gets wrinkles - but its crust is brittle, so it cracks, and one piece of crust is pushed up over the next. This makes small stair-step cliffs called fault scarps, typically tens of metres high and a few kilometres long. Shrinking may still be causing moonquakes: seismometers left by Apollo astronauts recorded 28 shallow moonquakes between 1969 and 1977, from about magnitude 2 to around 5. A NASA-funded study published in January 2024 placed the strongest shallow moonquake Apollo recorded in the south-polar region, where young faults lie near places Artemis astronauts may land - one of them inside a candidate landing region.

source_title: Shrinking Moon May Be Generating Moonquakes (NASA news release, by William Steigerwald, 13 May 2019)
quote: The Moon is shrinking as its interior cools, getting more than about 150 feet (50 meters) skinnier over the last several hundred million years.

extra_sources.title: Same release, the grape and raisin (NASA's own wording)
extra_sources.quote: Just as a grape wrinkles as it shrinks down to a raisin, the Moon gets wrinkles as it shrinks.

extra_sources.title: Same release, on the brittle crust
extra_sources.quote: Unlike the flexible skin on a grape, the Moon’s surface crust is brittle, so it breaks as the Moon shrinks, forming “thrust faults” where one section of crust is pushed up over a neighboring part.

extra_sources.title: Same release, on the size of the scarps
extra_sources.quote: These fault scarps resemble small stair-step shaped cliffs when seen from the lunar surface, typically tens of yards (meters) high and extending for a few miles (several kilometers).

extra_sources.title: Same release, on Apollo moonquakes

extra_sources.title: Shrinking Moon Causing Moonquakes and Faults Near Lunar South Pole (NASA, by William Steigerwald, 25 Jan 2024)
extra_sources.quote: The strongest recorded shallow moonquake had an epicenter in the south-polar region.

extra_sources.title: Same 2024 article, on the landing region
extra_sources.quote: One young thrust-fault scarp, located within the de Gerlache Rim 2, an Artemis III candidate landing region, is modeled in the study and shows that the formation of this fault scarp could have been associated with a moonquake of the recorded magnitude.

extra_sources.title: Same 2024 article, on the cause
extra_sources.quote: The contraction is caused by cooling of the Moon's still-hot interior and tidal forces exerted by Earth, resulting in global shrinking.

extra_sources.title: 10 Cool Things NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter is Teaching Us About the Moon (NASA Science, 24 June 2019, updated 26 Mar 2025)
extra_sources.quote: The Moon, long thought to be a dead, inactive world, is still losing heat and, as a result, shrinking.

extra_sources.title: Same page, on size and quake strength
extra_sources.quote: Some are fairly strong, reaching level 5 on the Richter scale used to measure earthquakes.

notes: Every part of the draft confirmed; wording cautions follow. (1) NASA's 2019 release says 'more than about 150 feet (50 meters)', not just 'about'; the 2019 '10 Cool Things' page says 'the Moon has lost 150 feet (50 meters) of width over hundreds of millions of years, scientists estimate' - so 'about 50 m' is fine on a card. (2) The grape-to-raisin comparison IS NASA's own wording (2019 release), and so is the next sentence about the brittle crust. (3) Keep 'may': the 2019 headline is 'Shrinking Moon MAY Be Generating Moonquakes' (the evidence: "eight of the 28 shallow quakes were within 30 kilometers (18.6 miles) of faults visible in lunar images"); the 2024 headline is firmer ('Causing'). (4) The magnitude range 'about 2 to around 5' is from the 2019 release; the 2024 article gives no number for the strongest quake - it only says its epicentre was in the south-polar region and that its exact location 'could not be accurately determined'. (5) The 2024 article (written when Artemis III was the planned landing) says 'Artemis III candidate landing region'; NASA has since re-planned Artemis III (see E16 in facts-environment.json), so on the card say 'a region where Artemis astronauts may land'. (6) The 2024 article adds a cause besides cooling: 'tidal forces exerted by Earth'. It also warns that 'some areas are susceptible to regolith landslides from even light seismic shaking' and that faults 'should be considered when planning the location and stability of permanent outposts on the Moon' - good hook for an outpost game. Both NASA pages are by the same NASA Goddard writer; the 2024 page was last updated 19 Mar 2025.

claim: On 12 December 1972, during Apollo 17's second moonwalk, astronaut and geologist Harrison 'Jack' Schmitt spotted orange soil near Shorty crater in the Taurus-Littrow valley and called out "There is orange soil!!"; his crewmate Eugene Cernan confirmed it. Back on Earth the soil turned out to be made mostly of tiny beads of orange volcanic glass, rich in titanium, which most scientists think were sprayed out by a lava fountain ('fire fountain'). NASA's sample guide dates the glass to about 3.5 billion years ago (3,480 million years).

Schmitt was 'the first trained geologist to travel to the Moon' (same NASA History page). The 12 December date is the NSSDCA photo caption; the NASA History page gives no calendar date. claim: On 1 August 1971, during their second moonwalk, Apollo 15 astronauts David Scott and James Irwin found a white crystalline rock at Spur crater, near their Hadley-Apennine landing site (Scott radioed: "Guess what we just found"). It is anorthosite - made almost entirely of one mineral, plagioclase feldspar - a piece of the Moon's ancient (primordial) crust. It was nicknamed the 'Genesis Rock' because it was thought to be among the oldest samples brought back; NASA geologists later concluded it is about 4 billion years old, although it is not the oldest Moon sample. Its NASA sample number is 15415 and it weighs 269 grams.

claim: By comparing before-and-after pictures from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (in orbit around the Moon since June 2009), scientists found more than 200 new impact craters that formed while the orbiter was watching, from about 3 to 43 m across - about 30% more than models predicted (a later NASA page says 33% higher). They also spotted over 47,000 small fresh marks they call 'splotches'. The top few centimetres (about an inch) of moon soil is being stirred up over 100 times faster than older models said - 99% of the surface gets overturned in about 81,000 years - so the Apollo astronauts' tracks will be gone in tens of thousands of years rather than millions, and long-lasting equipment such as a lunar base may have to be made sturdier.

notes: Corrections: (1) '222' is not on any NASA page I opened. NASA says 'over 200'; 222 is the count in the Nature paper as quoted by press coverage, and I could not open the paper (nature.com sent me to a login page). Print 'more than 200'. (2) '33% more' vs 'about 30% more': the 2016 NASA release says 'about 30 percent more new craters than anticipated'; NASA Science's 'Why Study Moon Craters?' page says 'a rate 33 percent higher than expected'. 'About a third more than expected' fits both. (3) 'In about seven years' is not stated on any NASA page I opened. NASA only says the craters 'formed during the LRO mission', which began in June 2009, and the study came out in October 2016. Say 'since 2009' or 'over several years'. Size: up to about 43 m is confirmed, and NASA gives a lower end of about 3 m (the SVS page says LRO's camera can see craters at least 5 m wide - a small inconsistency inside NASA's own pages). Base implication from NASA Science: such equipment 'would have to be able to withstand damage caused when nearby impacts spray debris that can move as fast as 1,600 feet per second (500 meters per second)'. The 81,000-year figure is for 99% of the surface being overturned, and the depth NASA gives for it is 'the upper few centimeters (approximately an inch) of the regolith'; the 2 cm figure is only in Emerson Speyerer's description of the old view (churning 'took millions of years to overturn the surface down to 2 centimeters (about 0.8 inches)'). Do not turn this into 'the whole Moon is dug up'. The 100-times speed-up is about soil churning, not about how many craters form.
